utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam Registrar. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams I don't see Mr. Haynes and I don't see Mr. Stojanovic. Otherwise everyone is present. The Defence [sic] I see Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls and Mr. Thayer. I understand there is a preliminary matter you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just something briefly that I should have sorted out and cleared up for the Court yesterday. You will recall that PW-111, the last witness, when I asked him a question about him giving us information that he had not told the doctors the complete truth because he was worried about his pension, and I think you followed up with a question, and he -- he said "no," basically. At that -- as you can imagine, I did have a basis for that question. And I had -- at that point I -- I didn't have the basis on my fingertips and I thought I might have mixed him up with another witness. Since that time, I have found the basis of that question, and I should have cleared it up with the witness yesterday, but he had, in fact, in a statement of 3rd December, 1998, told Mr. Ruez that very thing, that he had not told the doctor the whole truth because he was worried about his pension. I think he clearly had forgotten he had said that, but I did not want to leave that answer on the record without having cleared it up, and that's -- that's all I wanted to mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Does anyone wish to comment on that? None. For the record --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe just one thing I would like to say. I don't believe that this is the way, once the witness left to clarify things with what -- I have no problem with this, we are all aware of this, what Mr. McCloskey said. I just have a problem once the witness left that we discussed this issue. This is basically giving evidence on Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but it's not evidence in favour of the Prosecution, if anything. It would rather be evidence in favour of the Defence. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just want to say that I hope that my colleague will react the same way we are reacting today when something like this happens with one of the Defence witnesses. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I hope it won't happen again. For the record, Mr. Haynes has entered the courtroom. Yes. Anything else? No. So we can bring the witness in; first of the two. Incidentally, until he is ushered in, I asked you yesterday to check whether disclosure of the witness statement, that I referred to yesterday, has indeed been disclosed in November, as stated by the Prosecution, to all the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then could I kindly ask you, the Defence teams, since this witness is envisaged to start testifying, I think on the 28th or 26th or 28th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We are hoping around the 26th, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 26th of February. Could you be kind enough to file your response by the end of next week, by Friday, by today week, in other words. All right. Thank you. So good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of a solemn declaration you are required to take, namely, to testify the true. Please proceed with reading it aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. You are a Prosecution witness, and for that also a protected witness. We have put in place three protective measures, namely, the use of a pseudonym instead of your name, facial and voice distortion. I suppose these have already been explained to you. All I want to know is whether you are happy with this arrangement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. One other thing I wanted to alert you to is this: Since we have voice distortion, it is important that you don't speak when anybody else's microphone is on. So always allow a pause between question and answer, and if you notice that the red light -- if you look at me now, you will see what I'm referring to. You see that the red light on the microphone is on, don't speak. Wait until it's off. All right? We will be keeping a watchful eye, but this is all to protect you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls will be examining you first, and then we will have some cross-examinations. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I could hand the witness please P02441, the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Witness, could you just read that sheet silently to yourself and confirm that your name is printed on that sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If that could be shown to my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, as I explained to you, you are what we call a 92 ter witness, which means we will putting in a copy of your prior ICTY written statement and your testimony from your earlier appearance at this Tribunal. Now, in my office, did you read your ICTY written statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you make the following correction, which was at page 0077-8115 at paragraph 4: It is written there, "Every call, no matter what the subject or participant, was also in the notebooks." In fact, did you tell me that personal calls of no military significance were not transcribed in the notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Witness, with the assistance of an interpreter, because it was in English, did you review your entire testimony in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you made a correction there. This is at page 4544 at lines 5 to 7, you were asked a question about an intercept of 15 July 1995 at 9.52 a.m. which, Your Honours, is the same one at tab 5 in the packet 65 ter number 1177. The transcript in this section at line 5 to 7 states, "The participant was probably Colonel Beara who was looking for Zivanovic because that's what the text itself says. So the participant is Colonel Beara." Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what you wanted to correct in that answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Can I be provided with that text, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I can do that. We don't have it in English, but I can read out the question and answer to you. Again, this is at page 4544 of the transcript, line 3: "Q. This is a very short conversation and my question for you is the following: Can you tell me who was the participant in this conversation? "A. The participant was probably Colonel Beara who was looking for Zivanovic because that's what the text itself says. So the participant is Colonel Beara." Now, I don't want to lead you on this, but you told me in my office there was something you wanted to change in that answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I'm sure that it was Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Other than these corrections, can you attest to the Trial Chamber that your ICTY statement and the transcript of your testimony accurately reflect what you stated in the statement and in your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you also confirm and attest that your answers would be the same if you were asked the same questions today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please, for a short witness statement summary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In his statement and testimony, the witness described the process in which he would intercept, record, and transcribe VRS communications into the notebooks used at the northern facility. In his testimony, the witness authenticated eight intercepts which we -- which he had personally transcribed by hand. And these are also intercepts the Prosecution intends to tender in this case. The eight handwritten intercepts from the Krstic testimony which the witness authenticated are as follows: The Krstic Exhibit Numbers first, P330/1, which is 65 ter number 1169 in this case, and that's at tab 3 of the packet. P332/1, which is 65 ter number 1177 in this case, which is at tab 5. P333/1, which is 65 ter number 1178 in this case at tab 6. P334/1, which is 65 ter number 1179 in this case at tab 7. P335/1, which is 65 ter number 1187 in this case at tab 8. P337/1, which is 65 ter number 1189 in this case at tab 9. P338/1, which is 65 ter number 1204 in this case at tab 10, and P339/1, which is 65 ter number 1228 in this case at tab 13. I just read that out because it's -- otherwise it's difficult to match them up in the prior transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one question while we are at this. On the same page, because we were precisely coming back to you on -- on this because we look at page -- transcript page 4544 that you referred the witness to earlier on. Of course, at the top of the page, there was Exhibit 332 and we were going to draw your attention to that so we were not -- but further down the page, there is also reference to exhibits in the Krstic case, 331/A, 331/B -- /1 B, 331/1B. This is not amongst the ones that you have indicated to us now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I will have to check on that, Your Honour. 331/1 is definitely one of the ones in this case, and the As and Bs I would need to check again. I have them here, which version says R.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we need to know, because the B is obviously referring to the Serbo Croat language, I take it, so the indication should be towards 331/1. But we need to know whether that is also incorporated into the dossier that we have been given behind any particular tab so we will be able later on to follow the witness's testimony in Krstic to the full.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This -- I hate to admit it, actually occurred to me at about 3.00 a.m., that you may not have all the exhibits which are not ones that I intended to tender, which means that you might have some difficulty in following the testimony. But I -- that, as I say, occurred to me very late last night, and so we may need to supplement with -- with some of those because there were, for example, some photos in his Krstic testimony of recording equipment or antennas or something like that that I did not intend to go over again, but we can provide those to make it complete. What I've read out are all the intercepts in the packet which I intend to tender which he also referred to in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I have a few additional questions for you, sir. Not very many. First of all, do you recall that you reviewed 18 handwritten intercepts and the corresponding printouts of those intercepts in my office in a blue packet like the one I'm holding up with tabs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you also review the original notebooks containing the handwritten intercepts which were copied into this packet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you confirmed that the intercepts at tabs 1 through 17 were all transcribed by you and you recognised your handwriting in the notebooks as well for the -- for these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And here, in front of the Trial Chamber, could you please confirm that you intercepted, recorded, and transcribed the intercepts you recognised at tabs 1 through 17?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it's correct that you informed me that the last intercept at tab 18, dated 24 July 1995 at 10.35 a.m., was not in your handwriting, you did not transcribe that intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I didn't note it down and I didn't record it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just a few questions now about some specific intercepts. And could we first have -- I'm -- I'm going to ask questions about intercepts at tabs 5 through 8. Could I have 117C, the printout from tab 5 on e-court, please? 117C, excuse me. It might take a minute, Witness, but it should appear in a minute before you on the screen. There it is. Now, could you please take a look at this intercept. I'm interested in just the top portion and the first intercept at this time. What is the date of this first conversation which starts off in English "Colonel Beara," in your language "Pukovnik Beara"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Wait. Don't answer. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't believe there is any foundation. In fact, my colleague just said he's going to talk about the printout and I don't believe there is any foundation that this witness had anything to do with the typed version, he did the handwritten version, but not the typed version. So, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. He didn't have anything to do with typing this, but it's a printout of a conversation which he hand wrote. So I think it's fair to just show him this printout to -- it's a quicker way of establishing the date, which is already in the record, which has been submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think the matter that has been raised is easily solved. There is absolutely no reason why Mr. Nicholls should be stopped from showing the witness the printout. But there is also the copy of the transcript allegedly, as you say, in his own hand. And you can refer the witness to that. And then at the end of the day, if there are problems arising from either of these two, Mr. Meek has the facility to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I intend to show him his handwritten intercept as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question I mean, if you intend to ask him questions relating to the content, those three lines or two lines in the printout, there is no reason why you should select the printed version instead of the handwritten one. I -- of course you can ask him a question on the printed version too, if you have valid questions to put.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I wasn't going to ask him about the content, Your Honour. I was just going to establish that it is the same intercept and ask him what the date of the transmission was. That's all. The date the intercept was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perfectly valid question, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, if you look at this intercept, the first one, which begins "Colonel Beara," what was the date that this intercept was sent to the corps command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: The 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would like to now show the witness book 91, the original notebook. And if we could put this on the ELMO. I don't know if my colleagues want to see it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does anyone wish to see it? Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is P02329; that's the exhibit number for book 91.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, because I don't see it here, Mr. Meek is examining the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could have page 00800616 showing, that's the other page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the intercept which is now on the screen, also starting with, "Colonel Beara," could you please read that short intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: "Colonel Beara asked for General Zivanovic but he wasn't there, so they asked to call him on the local number, 139."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it's fairly clear, but can you tell me what the channel was and what time this intercept was recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Channel number 3 at 9.52 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, is this a summary or a verbatim transcription of the -- of this recording which you intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: This is a summary. He was asking for the exchange -- General Zivanovic at the exchange. He wasn't there and that is why he was told to call him on extension 139.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in your answer you just gave, who is the "he" when you state "he was asking for the exchange"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you just explain briefly, how did you arrive at the conclusion that this speaker was Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Probably at the time he introduced himself to the exchange and I could have recognised him on the basis of his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you, still looking at the same book, 91, P02329, which is on the ELMO, please read just silently to yourself the next intercept which goes from pages 00800616 over to 0617. And if it's easier for you, you can look at the handwritten copy of your book on -- which is to your right. Just let me know when you've read that next intercept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Again, this is 65 ter number 1178. Now at tab 6. If we could show the top of this intercept, where it begins -- if we could pull out a little bit. And if you can fit the whole heading in. A little -- pull out a little bit more, please. Thank you. That's good. Sir, what was the channel and time of this next intercept you wrote down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Also channel number 3 at 9.54.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And at the top, you have listed the participants as General Zivanovic and Colonel Ljubo Beara. My next question is, in this next intercept you wrote down, how did you determine that Colonel Beara was a participant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I recognised his voice and called him Zivanovic, General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You -- just to be very clear, you recognised whose voice when -- and who called somebody General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Colonel Ljubo Beara returned -- addressed General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to now ask you about the next intercept in that same book, P02329. This is the one that goes from pages 00800618 to 00800619. That is 65 ter number 1179, tab 7 in the packet. Could you just read this intercept to yourself, sir, and then -- silently and then tell me when you you've finished reading it. And just to be clear for you, sir, I'm referring to the exhibit -- the intercept where you've written the participants are Colonel Beara and General Krstic, and "(inaudible)"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just tell me again when was the time that you -- of this intercept and the channel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Channel number 3 at 9.57.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, the same question with this next intercept which you hand recorded, how did you determine that the speaker was Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, I could recognise his voice, but in this intercepted conversation, he introduced himself on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to show you one more intercept, that's at tab 8, it's 1187, but I want to show it to you in the book. The book is number 97, which has 65 ter number P02328. First, I should ask if my colleagues want to look at this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Meek is examining the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, sir. If you could please take a moment to read the intercept on page 00801263, which is before you. And again, if you need to pick up the book to read it, read it yourself in hard copy, that's fine. Just read the entire intercept and tell me when you're done.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Again, same questions: What's the channel and what's the time for this intercept, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Channel 3 at 11.11.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At the top the participants have been listed by you as Colonel Beara, Colonel Ljubo Beara, Cerovic, and X. Again, how did you determine that Colonel Beara was one of the participants in this conversation that you transcribed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, because they participated in this conversation. They are mentioned in these intercepted conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You mean Colonel -- Colonel Beara is mentioned in the conversation itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is not being broadcast, Witness, outside the courtroom. If you could look at the -- if we could go to the bottom of this page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will ask the question again, sir. Why is your signature -- don't worry, nobody can see it outside the courtroom. Why does it appear on the bottom right of this page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, whenever a conversation was intercepted, we operators, who were involved in the electronic combat, we would sign such conversations so that everyone could know who was working on a certain shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the previous intercepts which we looked at in the book today, your signature -- no signatures appear at the bottom by you. Can you tell us why that might be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't see it. Maybe we could have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, can I show it to you again, but maybe my colleagues will agree that there is no signature of his at the bottom of the other three intercepts we've looked at. And I just wonder why you're -- why those ones in your handwriting you haven't signed them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness has asked to look at these intercepts, and I think he should be able to. Number one. Number two, while he has these books, he should look at all the other intercepts he did not sign or did sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think he should be given the opportunity to have a look at the notebook, if he's asked for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. That's fine. And Mr. Meek can show him whatever he likes on cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you please look at 00800616 through 0619, sir. For the record, the witness is looking at P02329, which is intercept book number 91. Now, having reviewed that, did you see your signature on the bottom of those pages, which are the same pages we looked at earlier today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will just ask you again, can you give any explanation of why your signature doesn't appear on the bottom of those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Who is going first? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. Witness, when reading your statement I noticed that you said that you worked in shifts at your work post and they were daily shifts that lasted three or four hours. You do remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the shifts, but sometimes we had 12-hour shifts, it depended on our activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you said that too. You also said that, as a rule, one operator worked at night, whereas the day-time shift started at about 6.00 in the morning. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes, but it all depended on the activities, on the amount of work in the office itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Zivanovic, and Witness, please allow a short pause between question and answer. Although you are switching off the microphone before the witness starts, but still it's too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I also noticed that you said that the previous operator would usually inform you of the conversations he had heard during his shift and he would also inform you about whether the conversation was on one frequency and whether part of the conversation was on a different frequency. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition, I also wanted to ask you whether you could tell me something else, apart from the Srebrenica area, the wider Srebrenica area, Zvornik and beyond, I can see that you also monitored conversations in other areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, we did what they ordered us to do in the corps command. We rotated our antenna, depending on the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you something about the notebooks. Given the shifts that you worked, can you remember how many notebooks you had at your disposal at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. A lot of time has passed. Two or three notebooks. Perhaps every device had its own notebook, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you received those notebooks from your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Some from the command, sometimes someone would bring a notebook in. People did as best they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did those notebooks have some sort of a registry number provided by your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, we listed the number of the device on the cover and the date on which we first started using the notebook. As to whether they registered them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And tell me, as far as making notes in the notebook is concerned, did you have to make a note of the dates in the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: No, it wasn't mandatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And were you supposed to make a note of the frequencies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes. We made a note of the frequencies and also of the dates. If there was a lot of -- if there were a lot of conversations, if we didn't have enough time, well it was possible to establish which particular date was, in fact, concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If the conversation was interrupted in such situations, would you note down when the conversation was interrupted when you re-established a link between those participants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, if there was an interruption, we would make a note of that, or if you couldn't hear anything we would make a note of that, or if there was a lot of background noise we would make a note of that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And if, after a conversation had been interrupted, would you make a note of the fact that a conversation had been established between other participants? Would you write down their names if you knew of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Naturally I would write down the number of the channel and make a note of the participants if we could recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the frequencies too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since we've heard about the technology you used at work, did you ever put the information from the notebooks into computers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: There are various operators working in cryptographic protection who did such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, you didn't?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, perhaps on occasion, very briefly, if I was replacing a colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, when you worked on such occasions, did you write down the date yourself in the computer or did the computer assign the date itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, this was done manually, the date was registered manually in the computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In those reports, we saw that there were some numbers. Did the computer assign the number or did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Whatever was put in was done so manually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have information according to which those conversations on inputting were coded. Was that done manually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: My colleague was involved in cryptographic protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you did input text into the computer, you weren't involved in the cryptographic protection of that text?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: No. I was only helping my colleague to put the text in, but he was responsible for the cryptographic protection of the text itself, for the encryption of the text itself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that you have also mentioned laptop computers that you had at your disposal. What kind of laptops did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: It was an ordinary computer. As if children knew what a computer was in 1994. That was the first time I had seen a computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that laptop in 1999 when you gave a statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, it was a computer. Perhaps, I said that it was a laptop. Perhaps I named it as a laptop.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, it was an ordinary computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes, it was an ordinary computer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also said that you would make a note of urgent conversations in the notebook. Was that your assessment or did some of your superiors make such assessments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: We also made such assessments and our superior did so too, who was there with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain something to me. You would listen to these urgent conversations on a tape first of all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, yes. I would record it and also listen to it over the headphones and I could come to certain conclusions as to whether it was urgent or not and then we would immediately convey the information and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You made a note of the fact that it was urgent in the notebook, or rather, that it was urgent to convey such information to the command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the command only received this information through written reports that were coded in the computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, they received such information over the phone if it was urgent, or only subsequently, once the conversation had been noted down from the recording, then it was put into the computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If the command had then been informed of the noted conversation by telephone, can you tell me why the notebook stated also that the conversation was urgent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, because we assessed that it was urgent, that was our conclusion, so we made note of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier on you said that you would make a note of that, so that it could be urgently sent through the computer, but that is, in fact, not the reason for which it was noted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: That's not what I said. If the conversation concerned shelling, for example, the shelling of Tuzla, et cetera; it's an example, if I say Tuzla. Or in such cases, we ourselves would assess whether it was urgent or not. There wasn't time to put the information into the notebook. We would immediately phone the command, tell them what the situation was. For example, if coordinates had been provided, the population had to be informed so that they could take shelter, et cetera. And only afterwards would we note everything down in the notebook and state that it was a matter of urgency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I also see that you, when speaking of tapes, that you would receive erased tapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: When the tapes were completed, we would give them to the commander and receive new tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And there was nothing on the new ones, there was no conversation recorded on the new ones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Naturally, nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to examine one of the intercepts which you noted down. This is OTP 65 ter list number 1189.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Please identify A, B or C.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is P24/21.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel does not have microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is OTP tab 9. And it's marked here as 1189. B/C/S version. 1189B.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this particular intercept? Do you remember the intercept that is on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's the button --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please scroll down. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the conversation at the bottom, where it says 1358. Do you remember this conversation at the bottom, channel 3 at 1358 hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether this time was recorded afterwards, after the entire text was recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: You mean the time next to the channel? Well, it was noted down at the same time when the channel was noted down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you routinely record time in this fashion, sort of in a slanted way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, when pressed for time, you write as you can. It's not like we did it when I served in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean pressed for time? Were you pressed for time when recording time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but there was no rule specifying that we had to write it in one line. We could write it above or at the continuation of a sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain the reasons for not noting down the frequency here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: We noted down the frequency earlier, and then here we recorded only the number of the channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you did not record the frequency for each intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: The frequency is always the same. As long as it is active, it is always the same. As soon as there is a change, as soon as we notice that nothing is happening on a particular channel, then we would know that they changed the frequency and we would look for the new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this heading, we can see that there are two participants; Zlatar, duty officer there and duty officer in Palma, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the very bottom of the page you can see that there was an interruption in the conversation. Could we now turn to the following page? I can see that the participants are not recorded after this interruption. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, it says previously that there was an interruption in the conversation, and then the exchange asks, "Who is it?" It's on the following page. And then the response is, "Duty officer at Palma." So somebody marked the next person with an X, meaning unidentified person. And then they -- that person says, "Who do you need to speak to?" And then the rest is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the participants were the same and that, as a result of that, you did not identify them specifically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: No, I didn't know who the other participant was, the one marked with an X. Only those cases where I was fully certain would I identify the person as they introduced themselves. For example, I identified Palma with a P.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can we go to the previous page, please. In the previous page, these two participants are marked with letters Z and P, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now turn to the following page, please? The one we saw just now. Now, we have some participants here, one is marked with an X, one is marked with a letter B, and naturally, there remained the participant marked earlier with P. And after this interruption in the conversation, it seems to be that this is a conversation among different people, in addition to the one marked with a P.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Looking at the text, one could conclude that this was perhaps Zlatar, but since I wasn't sure, I didn't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, you started your cross at 9.48. That means you have just gone beyond the 20-minute. We will allow you two minutes more and that's the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need just one or two more questions, and I will finished with my cross-examination. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to tell you now that, again at the bottom of this page, it says again that the connection was disrupted, the -- there was an interruption in the conversation, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this is something that you noted down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: It is in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move to the next page, please? Do you see that we have yet another participant marked with a C, and we do not know who that person is, and the person was not identified in the heading at the beginning of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: This C probably stands for "centrala," the telephone exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can we please establish that somewhere midway through the page it -- there is a text in parentheses where it says, "Immediately after the conclusion of the conversation," and then it seems there is a new conversation. There is a letter G and that person says "hello" and then in parentheses, it says, "Immediately after the conclusion of the conversation" which means that what follows should be a new conversation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: This is a conversation on the same exchange, which means that the previous participants signed off and then the new ones continued. I think that this is all coming from Palma.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So it seems that there were three disruptions in these conversations, at least, that's what I was able to count. You didn't note down the time when the communication was re-established.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: These disruptions or interruptions were very brief. There was probably a break in communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Who is next? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you concerning your -- both your statement and some of the intercepts that you say you took down personally. My first question goes to, in respect of your statement, I would just like to confirm, because we don't see that whether it is in the statement or in your testimony in the Krstic case, that you received any specific training before you took up your position and started taking intercepts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I did have training. I became familiar with the equipment before we started working with them. We started with an ordinary Rup, R-u-p, and started intercepting with them and then we got these other pieces of equipment and some colleagues of ours knew how to work with them, so it was not difficult at all for us to work with that equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. So I take it that it was on-job training but you never attended a formal course with respect to the taking of intercepts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I worked on radio relay equipment back in the former JNA, and then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, can you repeat your answer again, because the interpreters didn't catch up the last part of your answer, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the equipment, I learned about it in the JNA when I had training, and then I had additional training in my ham radio club, and then yet another training, which I received when I started working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, I'm just going to go straight to the point. You did not attend a formal course before you started taking intercepts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think his answer -- I think he's answered that question, Mr. Bourgon. Let's move to more substantial matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President. But some other witnesses have said that they have attended a course, a 30-day course, and I want to establish that he did not attend this course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, my second question goes to the correction which you made this morning. My colleague referred you to something in your statement that you wish to correct. Now, I draw your attention to your statement, and I will quote from this statement, because on two occasions, you mention, and I -- this is the fifth paragraph on the -- on page 8115 of your statement, where you state, "All calls were recorded no matter what the subject or participants." So that's at one point. Later in the same statement it says again, "All calls were recorded." So I just wonder how come is it only today that you come and say well, no, not really all calls were recorded? Can you share with us, why is it that you only make this correction today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That wasn't the correction. The correction was about what calls were transcribed into the notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will check the transcript, but this is not at all what I have in -- neither in the notes that were given to me by my colleague, and I will quote from these notes. And I will also go back to the transcript at the beginning, and I hope that I will get more than 20 minutes to do my cross-examination because I'm going to waste some time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, while he is looking, I join in that objection because we're going find out in a minute exactly why we have to take this time, but you'll see. I join this objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In the notes that were received from my colleague, it says here, those are the notes from my colleague, it says the witness corrected the following portion of his ICTY statement at page 00778115, which is the page I quoted, and it says at paragraph 4, "It is not correct that every call, no matter what the subject or participants was also recorded in the notebooks. It is correct that every call was tape-recorded." So that's what I'm asking the witness to confirm now. And if I go into the statement itself, and I quoted two portions from that statement from page 8115, and it says, "All calls were recorded." And the first one it says also, "All calls were recorded no matter what."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I want to confirm, is it correct that all calls were recorded? That's my question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: All called were recorded on the UHER tape recorder, but we didn't take down silly things if somebody was dating somebody or things like that. And we also had papers where we recorded participants immediately, and later on we would see whether it was something that we should transcribe and put it in the notebook or not. But if somebody was just chatting up their girlfriends on the exchange, then we didn't need to write that down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now the reason I ask this question is that if all the calls were recorded on the tape, and then what you -- well, first, let's go with the first question. Transcribing the conversations in the notebook took place later and not immediately after the call was recorded. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if that is -- if that is so, and all calls are on that tape, it means that later on when you -- the time comes for you to transcribe a particular conversation, that it would be necessary for you to find that same conversation on the tape using your initial notes that you took. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: We would normally write down the number, when the conversation started, the number on UHER, and when it concluded. We recorded those numbers and we knew exactly at which number the conversation started, and at which it ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But these numbers do not appear, whether it's in your notes -- today I don't know these numbers -- what these numbers are, the start number and the end number of any particular conversation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: These are the numbers taken from UHER. We needed that number in order not to note anything on the tape, but to be able to know when the conversation started, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make this clear. You are referring to the counter on the UHER, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the counter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to -- I will skip the next two questions which were put to you by my colleague, and I move now to the next question, which is that when you had an important conversation that was taken directly to the -- to -- on the laptop before it was actually put in the notebook. Now, that's -- I refer here to page 116 of your statement. I would like you to confirm that in some cases the conversation was first put on the laptop before it was actually transcribed in the notebook. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I can't remember. It was long time ago. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But if -- if this is what your statement says, then that would be correct, because, of course, your recollection was better then than it is now; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: If that's what it says in my statement, that -- then it means that it's correct. But I can't remember, because it's been a long time. I can't remember what happened 11 or 13 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I fully understand, and I fully agree with you that it's very difficult for you to remember what might have happened while you were taking these conversations. I will have just a few questions before the break, and then I will move on. I have two intercepts to discuss with you maybe after the break. My first question is, I would like you confirm that it was always necessary for you to listen to those conversations many times before you could transcribe them in the notebooks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Naturally. When you are noting down something in the notebook you naturally have to play the tape back, because it's going too fast and you can't write down at the same speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, speed is one component, but the other component is that the quality of the tape was very bad and there was lots of interference. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Whenever we established that something wasn't clear, say something wasn't clear to me or I wasn't 100 per cent sure about a word, then I would call my colleagues and then I wouldn't tell them what I thought I heard, I would ask them to listen to that portion of the conversation. So, for example, I would call in one colleague, two or three, and then we would jointly conclude what we heard and note that in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So the content of -- of any particular conversation which was difficult to listen to is, in the end, the product of a consensus between you and three or four others and whatever you could conclude, then you said this is what we heard. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: As for the intercept, some were extremely clear, and intelligible. If I, as an operator, wasn't sure, then I would ask my colleagues for assistance, so we would decipher together what was said. For example, sometimes a word would be said in a less loud voice, or there was perhaps some background noise and this is what made it difficult to discern.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just refer you to your testimony in the Krstic case, and that was on page 4495, where it says, "Frequently we would get together, if we could not understand a word." So is it -- would you agree with me that it was more often the case that you had to ask your colleagues to go over an intercept than those intercepts which you say were clear? That was the exception rather than the rule; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I don't know how often that took place. I know that it wasn't true just of me, but also of my colleagues. They would ask for assistance in solving a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's exactly what I'm trying to get at, simply that it was a regular thing that you would help your colleagues or your colleagues would help you in trying to decipher what was on those tapes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This question has been asked a thousand times of other witnesses and has been asked several times to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is cross-examination. My colleague had better sit down. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think it's better to have a break. Let's have a break. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to take you to Exhibit 1177 Bravo for B. Can I have this one on the ELMO -- on the e-court, please. Witness, I have two questions in relation to this specific intercept, and a question was put to you by my colleague as to why this was written in the third person, maybe that was not the exact question, but that -- why it was written in such a manner. And my question to you is, because I referred to your statement, and that is on page 116. Sorry, on page 116. And where you say that "if the call was a general one such as this, I sometimes recorded it in this way." I would like to confirm with you, or if you could confirm that whenever we see a conversation written in that third person or this type of style, that this is indeed because this was a conversation you considered to be a general conversation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, there were often such conversations. Someone would be looking for someone. We wouldn't write down what was said. Let's say the other participant was there, so we just made a summary note. Colonel Beara was looking for General Zivanovic in this particular case. So we would briefly note such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that of course the -- if you had noted down the exact words which were mentioned on that occasion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Bourgon. One moment. Mr. Zivanovic, can you approach -- can you approach us a little bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies to you, Mr. Bourgon, but we needed to check something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, I will repeat my question, which is simply to say that, if you had noted down on that specific occasion the exact words which had been mentioned, there would be more to it than simply those three lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And with respect to this specific conversation, also in your statement on page 116, you mentioned that you could not be sure of the date, but that there was a way for you to try and identify the date, and that was by counting the number of days from this conversation to the next date which was recorded. And I quote your words. You mention, "I believe the conversation was on 15 July." My question is as follows: You also said in your statement that you can't be sure of this because even though you are counting backwards from the first date in the book, you mention, "I am not sure because another notebook may have been used in between." Do you recall saying this in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall, during your testimony in the Krstic case, where counsel for the Prosecution did an exercise with you, and I'm referring to page 4500 of the transcript, where basically he took you from the beginning of the book, looking at each conversation with the times, to try and determine the date of a specific conversation? Do you remember doing this exercise with the Prosecution in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I remember that I went back in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll try to make my question as precise as possible. First, I would like you to confirm that one of the ways which you believe it is possible to identify the date of a conversation is to look at the time of each conversation and to analyse this from the perspective of the first date which was put in the book. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But of course this exercise is not certain because, as you have said, another notebook may have been used in the meantime. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I don't think that any other notebook was used. Because this one was only used for that particular device and for these channels. We can see that all the channels here are the same. And everything was in order until the channel was changed and some other participant was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'll go to your statement, and that was on page 1116, and I would like you for -- to clarify this for us, where you say, and now I will quote the exact words: "I am not sure of this, especially as another notebook may have been used in between."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just, if there are going to be more questions on the statement about this area, if the witness wishes to look at his statement, I think he should be able to. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that should be adopted as a practice, each time the witness indicates his desire to look at -- Witness, do you wish to look at these notebooks or these parts? On the statement, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we should show it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely. I have no problem with that. It is on 7D90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And page 11 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's on page 8116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And this is -- yeah, is it in -- is it available in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, in B/C/S, sorry. That was the -- it would be better for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is not available in e-court at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I was told it was entered in the -- in the e-court. And my copy is -- I have...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it have a Prosecution number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 2440 is the Prosecution number, but it's not -- I don't believe it's in the e-court, unless -- because we were -- I have been told it was on 7D90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is in e-court as a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It is? Do we have it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 2440.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can we use it from the Prosecution, 2440, the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's already being done, Mr. Bourgon. Madam Registrar, it is important that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I have my microphone on. It is important that this is not broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is not being broadcast, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. In English it's 11 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: B/C/S version, Mr. President, the page is 7814. And that is -- and is the last -- the second last paragraph on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In your statement, Witness, can you see the statement on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The second paragraph on the bottom, I would just like you to, if you can -- sorry, it's the third paragraph on the bottom, whereas you say that on the 12th page of that book, now you are then referring to book 91, and that was the conversation channel 3 at 9.52 which was the one that was on the e-court, and you say here, "I'm not sure of this, especially as another notebook may have been used in between." And then you say, "But by counting the number of days," you believe that it was on the 15th. Can you explain this for us, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I think that it was a slip here in the statement when it says that another notebook was used. I think there was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that and I'll go to the next intercept, and that is on tab 2. And I would like to have on the e-court, please, 1165B for Bravo. Can you see this exhibit on your screen, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in this intercept we see that you have not identified, but you put at the top participants X and Y, which were both heard occasionally. My first question goes to, because in this -- in this intercept, two names are mentioned. And at the beginning where you attribute the sentence to X, it says, "Someone should find Drago Nikolic now and have him call Dzukic over here." I just want to confirm that looking at all the notes that I have here, as well as the notebook, that the name you that you did hear is in fact "Dzukic"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I move down on this intercept, because you mention at the top that Y was heard only occasionally, but at the end of the intercept where you have the speaker X, where it begins with "Yes, in Vlasenica" then we only have one speaker. I would like to confirm with you that everything that follows must be attributed to speaker X. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I understood from reading both your testimony and your statement, that when there was something that you did not hear you were -- the -- you were supposed to put three dots and some brackets or parentheses. So what I don't understand is how come you have all this text attributed to X but we don't know whether you heard anything in between those sentences. So am I to understand, from looking at this intercept, that you heard all of this from X and you could not hear anything from speaker Y? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: The lower part concerns X; those are X's words. And as far as Y is concerned, I didn't hear him anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But we can't tell if there was a pause or not between those sentences of X. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, there probably was a pause. When we took this down from the tape, we made notes in this way. We didn't use those dots.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So today, if I tried to know how long this -- this part, this conversation attributed to X at the end, where he is the only one that you can hear, it is not possible for me to tell how long this segment lasted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I don't know how long it lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's my point. I would like to move to tab 5, and that is -- sorry, tab 7. And to go to 1179E -- I for India on the e-court, please. This is a new intercept that we received yesterday, so that is not the one we want. 1179I for India, and it should be the one handwritten from the notebook. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I mean, when we deduct the time you needed to verify, interruptions and whatever, you have now been cross-examining the witness for 27 minutes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can I just say I have spoken to Mr. Josse. Neither defendants 6 or 7 are going to cross-examine this witness. I know you like advance notice, but it's no prejudice to them if Mr. Bourgon oversteps his time, and he is perfectly welcome to the time we would have taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, there are others. Mr. Meek, I suppose, needs some time. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We decided not to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't be needing more than 10 minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, we put down 30 minutes and I believe that will be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is not the question. There is the 20-minute limit that we imposed for intercept witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We understand, Your Honour. I will abide by the Court's order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Two questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's do it. You will have your 10 minutes or whatever time you require. Mr. Bourgon will be allowed to finish, and Mr. Meek will have the time he requires. And that should cover everyone. Correct. Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, I would just like you to draw your attention to this particular intercept which is on your screen, and I would simply like to confirm the same thing as we did for the last intercept, that everything we see with the letter B is attributed to the person identified as B, and we have no idea what the other person is saying on this intercept, because, as you say at the top, Krstic was inaudible. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my last question, Witness, goes to -- towards the end of this intercept, there is a word that is used and this word is "parcels." Now, in your statement you mention something about the word "parcels," and you said that this was a very common word in -- that you heard many times in many conversations, and that this could refer to weapons, to ammunition, or to many other things. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: That's correct. This was my assumption as to what there might have been in the parcels.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness P1172B -- THE FRENCH INTERPRETER: 1177B, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1177.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to this conversation that was recorded at 9.52 -- do you remember this conversation, or rather, the note you made of this conversation? Do you remember it today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: How do you expect me to remember after all these years?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Obviously you have no idea of the date on which you made this note.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Right now I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we now show the witness P1177C. When you were working in the army, did you have the opportunity of seeing reports of this kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: These are the reports that were sent to the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Have you -- or did you have the opportunity of seeing them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, as I said earlier, occasionally I would help my colleague type the report, and he would do everything else that was needed, meaning the encryption.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you typed out your reports, when you transcribed the conversations, did you make a note of the date and of the number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It may be me being slow, but I'm just not sure what number is being referred to, for clarity in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if this is a question of interpretation or not, but perhaps you can repeat your question, taking into consideration Mr. Nicholls's remark, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question concerns the date of the report and the number of the report, the number that is to the left, in the left-hand corner, in the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And one further thing. Did you make a note of the date and the number? Where? You are obviously asking him whether he made a note of that. Where would he make a note of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be more precise. What I'm interested in is to know whether the witness himself typed out the date and this number, or is it the person who was responsible for encryption who did this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. It's now more understandable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was done by the person who did encryption. That person put in all this data.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So would it be correct to say that a report of this kind is a report that you have never seen before, not in this form, you've never seen a report of this kind before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I did see the reports, as I told you earlier. Occasionally I would help my colleague by typing, but only the text portion.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you typed out the text, the upper part of the report was already in the computer? I'm referring to the date, the number, the addressee.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: No. They would insert it. It was not already in the computer. They would insert it. And I was only responsible for typing the text, and then they would insert the rest. But I did it only maybe once or twice, I mean, typed the text, without doing anything to the heading.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As far as this particular report is concerned, that relates to the conversation, you said that you couldn't remember the date of the conversation exactly. Is it correct to say that you never saw it before you went to speak to OTP investigators? You had never seen this particular report before speaking to the OTP investigators.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you didn't know who had typed it out on the computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, I know that. I told you, my colleague. There was a man who was responsible for encryption, and he would retype this and insert the date, the date that's in the heading, and that was always the same date that was in the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that as a rule [indiscernible] work, that in the case of this report, you have no means of confirming that this report had been, in fact, typed in the northern sector where you were located -- in the northern location.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: This report was typed in the northern location.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How is that you can confirm this? On what basis do you make such a claim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: In the heading it is stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And how did you know that someone hadn't taken this document later on and typed out a report of this kind after the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: No. Nobody knew what these reports would be used for. Nobody knew that they would reach this place here. It wasn't like we were playing with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not referring to you or to any of your colleagues. I'm just asking you how you can exclude the possibility of this report having been written after the war, regardless of how this was done or by whom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why, for what reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Your microphone. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
