utterances.text: I think he has explained everything he can about the typewritten report. He has explained his contact with it and how he drew his conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- let's approach this in the way it should be approached legally. Your question should be, to the witness, whether he has any knowledge at all that this report or others like it were typed out after the war and not during the time in which they are purported to have been typed out on the face of each document. And then the rest, if you want to bring evidence, of course you are free to bring evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply want to have an answer to my question as to how he can be sure that the report was drafted during the war, because my colleague from the Prosecution did say that the witness knew nothing about this report, but nevertheless, he asked him to confirm the date on the basis of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why we are telling you that your question should be the way we phrased it for you and not the way you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, would you allow for the possibility that this report was, in fact, drafted after the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Merci, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. How are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Thank you for inquiring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Meek. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, my colleague just asked you about the document 65 ter 1177C, and how the date got typed in there. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: As I said earlier, when it comes to inserting it on the computer, where the encryption was done, it was done by my colleague who was responsible for that part of the job. All I did was record intercepts, transcribe them, and note them in the notebook. I didn't enter or insert any dates. It was done by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I understand that, but I think you answered that the encryptor typed that date in from the notebook, from your notebook, and your handwritten transcription, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: He inserted or typed the conversation, and we didn't record dates in the notebooks all the time, because the transcribed conversations were immediately typed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, on page 47 you answered that, line 6, "He would retype this and insert the date, the date that's in the heading, and that was always the same date that was in the notebooks." Do you recall your answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: It's possible that I phrased it that way. Let me repeat it now. We didn't record the date in the notebook every time. For example, every intercept that was recorded on a certain day was encrypted afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, you never recorded the dates in the notebook, did you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: There was so much content that I think that we would need a truck to transport it. Now, as to exactly how many times we recorded the date, I wouldn't be able to tell you that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. But referring to this intercept, there was no date in the notebook, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I can't tell you until I have a look, because I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Would you like to look at the whole notebook, or the page that you transcribed in your own handwriting, the alleged conversation? Which one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: It doesn't matter to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May he look at the notebook real quickly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You want 00800616? That's the page you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's correct. And you might put that on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It says "CH-3", then "9:52," correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes, that's the channel number and the time of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me there is no date in your handwritten notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: It says at the top "channel 3, 9.52." There is no date, but the fact is, that this book, the notebook was opened or commenced on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I'm not going to go over the fact that you really don't know what date this was because my colleague has already done that. What I want to go to is your meeting with Mr. Nicholls from the OTP, and you met with him on two different dates this month, did you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you also agree with me, and I think you already have, that your recollection was much better back when you testified in Krstic case, for example, than it is today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I think yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that a long time has gone by and the longer that goes by your memory fades. You have already testified to that I believe, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, memory needs to be refreshed. It never fades really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, because on the 7th day of February, 2007, you met with Julian Nicholls and he refreshed your memory, didn't he, when he told you that in the Krstic case at page 4544, lines 5 through 7, that you had probably made a mistake when you used the word "probably" in line 5. Isn't that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment before you answer. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I object to that question. There is no basis for it. I didn't say that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I object to him putting the answer in this witness's mouth, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I object to him with no basis and no foundation whatsoever making before this Court statements which he alleges that I made, words that came out of my mouth. Unless he has some foundation for it, I object to words being attributed to me which I did not make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment. Mr. Meek, I think we need to have you clarify this first. On what basis are you maintaining that when the witness met with Mr. Nicholls, Mr. Nicholls told the witness that in the Krstic case at page 4544, lines 5 through 7, the witness had probably made a mistake when he used the word "probably"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the witness take his headphones off?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you understand English, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So could you remove your headphones for a while, please? What you are suggesting is that the statement that ultimately it seems the witness volunteered to Mr. Nicholls, namely, that that excerpt on page 4544 needed to be corrected on his part, was not his own reaction to reading the transcript itself, but a prompt from Mr. Nicholls himself. This is what you are suggesting. So what we would like to know from you is on what are you basing this, because you can obviously ask the witness if Mr. Nicholls prompted him to make the correction or whether it was an impromptu one on the witness's part. But if you are suggesting that Mr. Nicholls -- you are not putting the question to the witness, you are making it a statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe the question actually was not phrased properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But my foundation for it is the fact that, and it will come out later, this witness doesn't remember any of these conversations. He said it in his statement; it will come out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's fine. Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we will close this chapter and you will rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just want to make clear, my objection is to specific words attributed to me. He has made the allegation that I said to the witness, you probably made a mistake, and I asked him to change it and nothing has happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you are 100 per cent correct. If that is true and Mr. Meek has a foundation, then obviously he can proceed along those lines. But he hasn't provided us with...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Incident closed. I don't want to blow it up beyond what is necessary. Yes. Witness, don't answer the previous question. The substance of the question is going to be rephrased and then you answer the -- this new question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, before I get to this question that I'm going to rephrase, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor back in 1999, 7th day of May. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I think it was in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You are correct. May of 1999. Now, in that statement, and for the Court and the record, 8115 would be the ERN number. You stated at the bottom that you can't remember now if you had a notebook for each machine. Do you remember saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. The next page, the English version, 8116, again for the record, it's 65 ter 7D90. When you were discussing or giving your statement, you stated that you were not able to remember the exact conversation that took place allegedly on what you claim is the 15th of July at 0954 hours. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown on e-court 65 ter 2440, that's the B/C/S statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would need to take it off so that it is not revealed to the public.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is not being broadcasted at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to put the witness's mind at rest that you must have heard me before making sure that any such document is not broadcast. So put your mind at rest that no one else is seeing it outside these four walls, except of course the technicians that are recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In the B/C/S version, it's probably the last page or the second to the last page. It would be the last page in B/C/S. No, before. One more page before that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You see the paragraph that starts with, "The next column of the book is also mine and is headed, 9:57 CH 3"? Please scroll higher. Do you see the paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And just take a moment to read it. Have you finished, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, when you gave this statement it was read to you back in your own language, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You signed saying that you understood it and that everything in there was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection, did you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You do not remember that conversation, do you? You didn't remember it then in 1999 and you don't remember it today, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: When I looked at these documents I became able to remember the conversations, some conversations. As for what it says here, that only one participant in this intercept could be heard, this was in a duplex mode, which means that the other participant was on another channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just want to make it clear for the Court, and I think it's fair that the portion of the transcript which counsel is directing the witness to is a different intercept than the one he began this line of questions of, which was at 9.52. So he started off talking about that one with the witness. He has now directed the witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm going to clear it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The document we're talking about is the one allegedly between Beara and Krstic who you could not hear, who was inaudible, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To simplify matters, that is available -- if that intercept is available, let's show it to him. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sure, it will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: 65 ter 1179C, I think, or B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we have a hard copy of it, it's better so that the rest of the statement remains on the screen, for him to be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the book is in front of him on the ELMO, and this conversation is allegedly two minutes after the one before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you help him, Madam Usher, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's there right now, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You see on the ELMO, sir? And again, "channel 3, 9.52." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I see channel 952, 954, which means channel 3, but not channel 3 at 9.57.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And again, if you just go one page back in the notebook you get to the alleged intercept that you say came in at 9.54, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And right above that is the 9.52 intercept, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, I believe you've already testified in cross-examination that you don't remember the 9.52 conversation, that it was -- you just synopsised it, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I wrote this down, which means that I heard Colonel Beara talking to somebody asking to speak to General Zivanovic. So I noted it down briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. But if we go back, flipping one more page to the 9.57 -- no, the other way. The alleged conversation at 9.57, channel 3, where you say Krstic is inaudible, you gave a statement and you said you do not recall this conversation happening. And that was true when you told the OTP that, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the conversation. This isn't the only intercept. How could I remember all of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, that's fair. Now I would like you to look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll withdraw it. I will just leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Maybe we can do this on e-court. It would be 65 ter 1187 in English, probably 1187A in the handwritten B/C/S version. Could they be put on the screen for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, do you see those on the screen, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And on the right-hand side is handwritten, and 1263 as the last ERN numbers. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I didn't understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you see on the right, is that your handwriting on the right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you gave a statement to the OTP back in 1999, you did not recall that conversation at the time, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I didn't then. As I already told you, I can't remember until I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you telling me and this Court that they didn't show you these documents when they -- when you made your statement in 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Sir, it seems that you are asking me to quote from each of my intercepts. When I see the original material in front of me, then yes, I can recognise my handwriting, the way I wrote down paragraphs, and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Maybe it's a matter of interpretation. My question is simple. They showed you this notebook and they showed you this entry when you gave your statement, and you said, "I do not now recall this conversation, but again, I am sure I recorded it correctly from the tape of the conversation." That was in 1999 when the Office of the Prosecutor showed you that notebook, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: If that's what it says there, then it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, I'll just ask that the Prosecutor stipulate that's exactly what he said in his statement in 1999 about this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can do that. This is in evidence. I mean, the Court and everybody else is going to be able to read it. It's been submitted. It will be submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The statement is going to be submitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So my question to you is, if in 1999 you couldn't remember these conversations actually taking place, but when you looked at your handwritten notes you said, yes, those are my notes, so therefore what I wrote down must have been said, that's what I heard; isn't that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Everything that is noted down here in the original, everything that is written by me, is a true reflection of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Then, sir, you came as a witness in the Krstic case, and when you were asked about the conversation that -- which we were talking about earlier between allegedly Beara and Zivanovic, you stated, "The participant was probably Colonel Beara who was looking for Zivanovic because that's what the text itself says." Now, you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to see the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Either show him the text, I would say, or show -- the complete answer would be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but the witness has already shown -- indicated that he wishes to see the text, so let's show him the text first, and then if necessary --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: He doesn't speak English, and I don't have a B/C/S copy of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You can just read exactly the entire answer, not just the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The question that was put to you in Krstic, sir, was: "Q. This is a very short conversation and my question for you is the following: Can you tell me who the participant was in this conversation?" Your answer: "A. The participant was probably Colonel Beara who was looking for Zivanovic because that's what the text itself says. So the participant is Colonel Beara." Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I would have to have a look at that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, you met with Julian Nicholls, the Prosecutor, on the 7th of February, and apparently you told him that you really were mistaken in using the word "probably" and that you are certain that the participant was Colonel Beara, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I am requesting that you show me the document, and then I will give you a concrete answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's put it on the ELMO, but it's not going to be of much help, because this is -- this is in English. What you are going to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's not a clean copy, and if you want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, but I think it is in the e-court in any case. But the thing is I don't know what you mean by saying that you want the original, because this is a copy of the transcript of the -- your testimony in Krstic, and it's in English. I mean -- unless there is -- there is a copy in your own language, which can be made available and no condition that it is a faithful translation of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We don't have it, as you say, Your Honour, in B/C/S. That's -- I'm not sure the witness realises that, that there isn't a copy in his language. This is the only copy we have. The audio is also disclosed, but has not been played to the witness. He -- it was gone through with the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May I put the question to this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, he can see the document now, for whatever it's worth to him, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is it on the e-court system?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Page 4544.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- not yet on the e-court system, no. And it's not on the ELMO either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, you wanted to see this, now you have it in front of you. And start at line 3. 1, 2, 3, the third line down. And it says "Q."; do you see that? And that means a question by the Prosecutor. "This is a very short conversation, and my question for you is the following."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be correct, fair to the witness, this is not a question by the Prosecutor. This is cross-examination he is reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise. This was a question put to you -- and I'm going to start reading it again. Do you see where line 3 is, Witness? Can you read any English at all, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. What about numerals, 1, 2, 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. You see where it says line 3, there? You see that, sir? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, let me read it in English, and it will be translated in B/C/S, okay? Question put to you in cross-examination in Krstic: "Q. This is a very short conversation, and my question for you is the following: Can you tell me who the participant was in this conversation?" Line 5, your answer, under oath: "A. The participant was probably Colonel Beara who was looking for Zivanovic, because that's what the text itself says. So the participant is Colonel Beara." Now, do you remember that, sir, when you testified under oath in Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I remember that. I remember that I testified, in fact, but I can't remember this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you told the truth in Krstic, didn't you? You told the truth in Krstic, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I always tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I always tell the truth and nothing but truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then, sir, tell me how it is, 11 years after this alleged intercept was taken by you, that you suddenly remember that seven years ago when you testified in Krstic that it was a mistake to use the word "probably" in line 5? How did you come about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I remember General Krstic's trial, but I can't remember my testimony with precision, but everything that I said is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So if it was the truth that it was probably Colonel Beara, is it also the truth when you told Julian Nicholls from the OTP on February 7th of this year that you made a mistake when you used the word "probably" in the Krstic trial? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I can't remember. I'm a bit under pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, sir, we're all a bit under pressure. I assume, on February 7th, when you were sitting in the office somewhere with Julian Nicholls having a cup of coffee, you didn't feel real pressure, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I have been under pressure since I came over here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: One question. I'm done with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Who came up with the idea that when you used "probably" in the Krstic trial, that you were mistaken? Who came up with that idea on February 7th of this year in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Perhaps if I read through this testimony I noticed that a mistake had been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you read through the testimony, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes, I read through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You read through it or it was read to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I read it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And what language did you read it in, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: In my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My question to the OTP is simply, do they have a copy of this testimony in B/C/S? They represented they don't a while ago on the record, and I want to know if they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, sir, when did you first hear Mr. Beara's voice? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I can't remember. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you tell me what characteristics in his voice that he had that made you recall it and know it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I can't remember at this point in time, but from 1992 until 1996, all the participants in the network were participants I could recognise on the basis of their voices. It wasn't even necessary for them to introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you knew each and every participant by their voice without having to be introduced or having been introduced? Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary for them to introduce themselves. I could recognise whether it was Beara, Krstic, Zivanovic, et cetera. But we made notes of matters in the notebook as you can see. For example, Colonel Beara and General Krstic has been noted down here, and then it says that you can't hear Krstic. So I just made a note of what Colonel Beara said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you have answered the question. It was put to you that you must have heard, over this time, a lot of persons speaking or talking, and the question is, are you affirming here that you recognised the voice of each and every one of these many persons that you heard talking or whose conversations you intercepted or only of some?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to explain. I think Mr. Meek is owed a clear answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, explain this, because you just answered to my question a while ago under oath and you said you knew everybody. What is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The reason why I put the question is precisely because I disagree with you, Mr. Meek, or I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is the first time I have done it in this Tribunal. I object to his manner with the witness. The witness has said that he is feeling a bit of pressure. I think the witness is trying his best. There is no need to raise his voice and make those gestures, and really, insult the witness in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let the record reflect he is pointing at me, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct. The record is correct. There may be some more pointing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think when it's time, and hopefully it will never get to that stage, when the witness needs to be protected we will intervene. Don't worry about it. Witness, did I make myself clear? You answered "da" but I think "da" needs some further explanation. Let me make it even simpler. If over this period of time you heard or you intercepted the conversations say of 100 persons, are you stating here today that you could recognise the voices of each and everyone of those hundreds persons or of only some of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I could recognise most of their voices, starting with Beara, Krstic, Zivanovic, Borovcanin. I can't remember all of them now. I can't list all of them, but I knew most of them on the basis of their voices. I could recognise most of their voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Witness, but I will point to the Court, page 65, line 12 through 15, Witness, you just answered -- you said, "from 1992 until 1996, all the participants in the network were participants. I could recognise on the basis of their voices. It wasn't even necessary for them to introduce themselves." Are you taking that back now, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: That's what I said, that I could recognise their voices. Well, then that is the case. And I could recognise the participants. As soon as a signal was captured, it means the network was activated. As soon as a participant was heard, I was able to recognise the participant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just to be clear, did it take you any time to recognise the voices or the very first day you were there you got an intercept and you knew it was Zivanovic without him introducing himself or anybody saying his name. Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: When I started doing that work I couldn't immediately recognise the voices. The participants had to introduce themselves. It's only after some time had passed, let's say about a year, it's only then that I was able to recognise the voices of the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So to make this even clearer, you started doing this at this location in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I apologise. At the northern location. We were at another location before, and I think that we moved to the northern location in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, approximately how often did you hear Mr. Beara's voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Well, it was quite frequently. I can't remember how often exactly, but quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So the Prosecutor has given us, if I am counting correctly, four separate intercepts by you where you allegedly heard Mr. Beara, for your testimony today. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I don't know how many he provided you with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, you sat with -- two days with the OTP and you went through these intercepts, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes, I went through them, but I can't remember anything anymore. I went through all the conversations. I even said that one of the transcriptions wasn't mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And if I tell you that there were only four intercepts where allegedly you heard Mr. Beara, would you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I don't think I would agree with that. I think that there were more such conversations, more such intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I would ask you why the Prosecutor didn't put all those more in there, but you don't know that. Could you show the witness, please, 65 ter 1187B, I believe. And A is the English. Witness, you see these now, these pages? On the right, ERN number 1263 on the top says "channel 3, 11.11".

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is not being broadcast now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Who is the participant Cerovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Are you putting that question to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, yes, you are the one answering questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Colonel Beara and Cerovic are the participants here. I can't remember exactly who Cerovic was. I can't remember what position he occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And who is X in this conversation, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: A person who probably hadn't introduced himself or herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you see that about five lines down there is a word, "Triage has to be done on the prisoners." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In fact, that word is used three times in this alleged intercept, is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Four times. The word "triage" is used four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Did you often hear that word used when you were intercepting conversations and listening to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I can't remember whether it appeared in any other intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the actual notebook that this handwritten -- his handwriting is in? It may be -- it may be next to him, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: While we're looking for that, Witness, you've already told us that the use of the term "parcels" was a code word. So I'm asking you now, what was the word "triage," what did it mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I don't know what the word means. What was heard was what was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, what date was that, sir? What date -- you're looking at the original notebook. There is no date on that page, is there, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: The 14th of July. It would be possible to figure out the date because on the 14th of July, well, that's the date when the notebook was first used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear on this, this was the 14th day of July, that you took this alleged intercept?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I -- I won't object. I don't think that's at all what was said, but...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, let me just ask you this: Just a moment ago you answered, you said, when I asked you the date, because it wasn't on the page, you said: "A. The 14th of July --" For the record, it is line 11, page 70. You went on to say, "It would be possible to figure out the date because of the 14th of July. Well, that's the day this notebook was first used." So I want to clear it up. This intercept was taken by you on the 14th of July, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. All I can say is that the notebook started being used on the 14th of July. As for the date of this intercepted conversation, well, I couldn't say exactly, but I think that one could figure out the date. I assume that this would be possible. I think it would be the 15th or the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, I want to make this clear. I want to understand that when you would finish a notebook, you would turn it into the platoon commander, correct? Or it was placed in a cabinet by the platoon commander and later, depending on the urgency, the tapes and books were taken to the 2nd Corps headquarters for their review. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes, we handed the notebooks over to him. He would keep them in his office, the notebooks and the tapes, and later they were probably taken up to the corps command, or rather, it's not that they were probably taken up there, they were certainly taken to the corps command archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you never saw them again after you gave them to the platoon commander, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: No, not until I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you do not know who had access to that cabinet that the platoon commander put those notebooks in, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: It was his office, and only he had access. He alone was there; we never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. We'll -- yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could, just for the record, at page 71 at lines 8 and 9, the witness was saying, "I think it would be possible to figure out the date," and then the last line of the answer is, "I think it would be the 15th or the 16th." I just wanted the record to reflect that before he gave that last answer, he was looking at the notebook and flipping through pages. Otherwise it won't be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that out. We could see that and we confirm it. Thank you. We will have a break now. And for -- of 25 minutes. Maybe we can -- we can handle that stage now. Do you have a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the testimony of this witness, the name of my client was raised and I kindly ask for the opportunity to cross-examine just very briefly, couple of minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, after the break. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We just wanted to inform you that I need to be away this last session, or a major part of it. So we will be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. I have to attend to a personal problem. And Judge Kwon will be presiding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. As was informed, we will be sitting pursuant to 15 bis. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Before we went to the break, when speaking of the persons whose voices you recognised, on page 67 of today's transcript, you listed certain participants, including Borovcanin. Let me ask you this first: Was this a slip of tongue, or do you maintain that you recognised the voice of General Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I recognised voices. I enumerated names. Roughly, I can't remember all of the names of the participants, but I did recognise all of the voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So when you said Borovcanin, among other participants, did you refer to General Ljubomir Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have just a couple of more questions to clarify, that if you recognised somebody's voice that was a result of having heard that voice many times before, so that you became familiar with the intonation and certain features of the voice, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm speaking in hypothetical terms. If you heard General Borovcanin many times, I suppose that you would have noted down some of his conversations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-157
utterances.text: We wrote down all of the conversations. Right now I just can't remember. Perhaps I mentioned Borovcanin's name accidentally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Nicholls, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have a brief question to the witness. I'm not sure whether this is an appropriate question to put to you, Witness, but I wonder if you know by any chance the method, how the typed versions or encrypted versions of intercepts were sent to Tuzla, or command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that these encrypted conversations were sent by computer. Some kind of computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What do you mean by "computer"? Did you have Internet access, and then you sent them by e-mail, or it -- how?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. To tell you the truth, I don't know. All I know is that all information was sent immediately to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, and I would like to thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we deal with exhibits? I understand these -- this has been distributed to the Defence. I wonder whether there is any objection in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Prosecution wants to tender in tab -- excuse me, Judge. I think it's tab 16. Frankly, the witness didn't even mention it, and Mr. Nicholls -- yeah, tab 16, 65 ter 1310. Some alleged intercept at 0805 hours. It's got a 2475 ERN number on it. Never mentioned, number one. Number two, the Prosecutor said we're going to deal with eight intercepts, tab 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did they not confirm with the witness that 17 intercepts were those transcribed by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What is the basis to bring it in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not our practice? I was specifically reminded by Judge Prost that Mr. Nicholls referred from tab 1 to tab 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could say something to be clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I confirmed that those were his intercepts in his handwriting. What I said was I was going to ask questions about tabs 5 through 8, not about eight intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, as long as the record reflects that the intercepts that this witness actually testified about are the only intercepts that he alleged heard my client's voice, or who he thought was my client's voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber does not think the Prosecution has to go through each and every intercept they are going to produce. They are entitled to deal with these certain intercepts, they like to emphasise or -- so the objection is not sustained. Any other objections? So those will be admitted pursuant to the prior practice, so intercepts will be marked for identification and those -- those in bold letters will be put under seal. In relation to the question I put to the question [sic], have we heard that kind of evidence so far, as to the actual method, how those were sent to the command? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe we -- we have -- we could go into private session, I can...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will do that. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you kindly take the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I haven't heard any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Sir, you -- you have a protective measures of voice distortion and face distortion, so that you will not be recognised outside the courtroom, and also you will be referred to as Prosecution Witness 157. Do you understand that? Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, he has another protected witness pseudonym, PW-145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just saw the number of the previous one. So you will be referred to as Prosecution Witness 145. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Madam Usher is handing --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- read it to yourself please and confirm that your name appears on that page along with the pseudonym PW-145. For the record, the pseudonym sheet is P02431.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we met earlier in the week and a witness statement was taken from you at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was that statement read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you sign it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you attest, before this Trial Chamber, that the contents of that witness statement are true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, can you further attest that the answers would be the same if you were asked those same questions here in court today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm going to do now is read a very brief summary of your witness statement, which was taken on the 6th and 7th of this month. And I will keep it generic enough, so I believe we will be able to stay in open session for the entire summary. The witness is a Bosniak Muslim. He completed electro-technical high school in 1981. He performed his mandatory JNA service in 1982 to 1983. And the witness became a ham radio enthusiast in 1978, competing in amateur radio competitions between that year and 1985. The witness also holds a B category ham radio certification. In April 1992 the witness began serving in a signals and communications unit of the State Security Services of a CSB located in Bosnia and Herzegovina. While in the same unit, he began working regular shifts at the northern location in approximately the end of January 1995. The witness described their shift structure, the equipment they used, and the procedures they followed to intercept and transcribe conversations. The witness reviewed 23 typewritten intercepts and confirmed that he was either the recorder/transcriber or the typist/cryptographer for each of them. The witness's code-name appears at the bottom of each intercept, along with the name of his colleague. And for the record, the OTP witness statement is P02430. Now, sir, in preparing for your testimony today, did you review a packet containing material pertaining to -- or containing material pertaining to 23 intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And specifically, sir, did that packet contain typewritten printouts of 23 intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, were you able to confirm whether or not those 23 intercepts were conversations which you either recorded and transcribed or typed and encrypted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And finally, sir, are the 23 intercepts contained in the packet which you reviewed the same intercepts that were just referred to in your OTP witness statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Who will go first? Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Since the two of us speak the same language, in order to protect your identity, would you please not start speaking until I turn off my microphone. You will see when the red light is off, then you should start speaking in order to protect your voice.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the statement you gave to the Prosecutor you mentioned a piece of information, namely, that in the report which you sent to the superior command, you would normally put in information that you received from the BiH army. Do you remember stating that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When putting in that data, did you listen to the conversation that you received from the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you use the same equipment or you had separate equipment through which you listened and transcribed intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: You mean the same equipment as the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Roughly it was the same equipment. It was not a professional equipment, but rather amateur equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When recording and transcribing these conversations and when producing your reports, in the heading you would always insert -- insert certain data and this preceded the text of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in that heading, you would normally include the frequency of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And participants in the conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes, if they were known at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And if you couldn't hear some participant, you would duly note that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And if you did not record the conversation from the very beginning, you would note that down as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now show to the witness Exhibit 6D41. Sir, I don't know whether this is your intercept, but this is an example of a heading, and I would like to see whether this is how you typically produced headings. You will see it on the screen, and then you can confirm it. See here, the paragraph that begins with the words, "On the 9th of July." Were you able to read this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a typical example of how you worked, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Roughly. There are some differences in the form, but roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now show the witness 65 ter document 1096?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Could the counsel please specify if it is A or B, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, in the document that we received, it is not marked as B. The only mark it has is ERN 03201098, 03201098.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's part of tab 2, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, tab 2. Not this one, but the following one. 03201098 is the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The one on the screen is 98.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1099.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember transcribing this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we not show the previous page, the bottom part, "Broj 535"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely the right one. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you transcribed this conversation too, or recorded this conversation. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here in the heading it is stated that you didn't hear the other participant.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you look carefully at this conversation, you will see that the name of Karadzic is not mentioned there at all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Can I see the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be shown the entire conversation, please? Please look at it. It's in front of you. In the first conversation and in the second conversation, if you look carefully, you will see that Karadzic is not mentioned anywhere. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree with you. But you can see that he is addressing the other person with "The President."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So based on that, based on the fact that the word "President" is mentioned in the conversation, you concluded that the other participant was Karadzic and that's why you put in his name. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Well, the title of "President" is mentioned. Typically, this way of addressing the person holding that office, and you know how normally with what respect somebody addresses their president, we concluded that this other person was Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could it have been some other president?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: I don't think that it could have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Well, because, given the events at the time when these things were happening, well, you will see from subsequent conversations, if you had a look at all of them, that at one point in time we emphasised the fact that Mr. Gvero was in the Main Staff on his own. In fact, I don't mean that he was actually on his own, but he was the only superior member of the Main Staff present. And everything he said at the time was conveyed to his immediate superior. We knew that all the new information was directly conveyed to the president, that is to say, to Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But that's your assumption. It's not contained in these conversations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Well, my assumption, given all the time that has passed, it's a little difficult to say because there are quite a few of other conversations that haven't been seen here, conversations in which it was quite clear as to who was addressing whom. So it's difficult to say, but believe me, even now I'm certain that Karadzic was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But in the conversation that you intercepted, the information that you were referring to was not present. This is just your conclusion, your assumption, a conclusion you have reached on the basis of analysis of your own.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes, it is a conclusion on the basis of analysis of previous conversations and of all other conversations. We knew how people were addressed, how certain people addressed others, and we knew what was done on certain channels.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 6D43. Unfortunately, Your Honours, we obtained this document yesterday. It's a Prosecution document, so we only have the B/C/S version, and we have a hard copy. So we'll ask the usher to show the witness this document and we have copies for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. In the meantime, can I ask the witness to clarify what he meant by -- when he said, "Mr. Gvero was the only superior member of the Main Staff present." Present where? Sir, could you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that's what I said. Present in the Main Staff of the then RS army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think I follow in full. I don't think you mean that he is the only person present in the Main Staff. If Mr. Krgovic could pursue on this matter further. I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just refer back to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the screen. It says, "General Gvero is present in the Main Staff today." In the main command, in the Supreme Command Main Staff. That's what it says here. Please have a look at the document on the ELMO, not this one but the next one. Have a look at the document that you have in front of you. Can you see that another president is mentioned here as well, and he is being addressed with respect. Read through that conversation and just focus on these sentences in which Gvero is apparently addressing that president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm just wondering if there is a date that could be attached to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic. And if I can say this, it is very difficult to follow the -- for the non-B/C/S reader. So if you could ask the witness to read out the relevant parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Should I read it out, or will you do so? Will you read the relevant parts out loud? Your Honours, with your leave, I will read them out. I think we will be able to get through them more rapidly in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a question mark and that's how the conversation starts. "Hello. Good day. Good day. Gvero. How are you, General? How are you? Well, I'm fine. Is the president there? Well, the president is outside. He's not in the room. He will be here in 10 minutes' time. Is there a message you would like to leave?" I don't want to read through the part that starts with the letter G. "Greetings president. Gvero. Greetings, General."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that General Gvero is speaking to another president and is also addressing him in terms of respect, as you yourself said? Would you agree with me? I can see you nodding.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: But just explain on what basis you draw the conclusion that Krajisnik is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's your service's conclusion too, because in the upper right-hand corner it says Krajisnik, but the name Krajisnik isn't mentioned anywhere in the conversation. So this is just another assumption that Krajisnik is, in fact, concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, in line with my request for some sort of date on this document, we haven't established that this witness can recognise this as one of his sites or has any other familiarity to authenticate what this particular printout is purporting to be. So I just ask for perhaps a little bit more basis to be laid for, for example, the last question, where it was put to the witness that it is his -- I believe his army's assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought the witness was able to -- would be able to deal with the question as far as the president is concerned. But, Mr. Krgovic, could you clarify the date, or could you answer to -- answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can. This document is dated the 28th of April, 1994. It was in the Prosecution bundle of documents. I found it in the IDS -- in the EDS system, and that's why it hasn't been translated yet. It has an ERN number, so it can be located, and it is part of a collection of documents, a group of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you have a look at the frequency to the left, if you have a look at the direction, are you familiar with this frequency and with the elements that we can see to the left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Well, the frequency isn't one that is familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Can you see the frequency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown Exhibit 6D21?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long do you think you will stay longer with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, about another 15 minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have we received the time allocation amount of Defence counsel? I haven't received one. Proceed in the meantime. 6D21.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document from the service that you worked in and forwarded certain documents to this Tribunal. Could the witness be shown the third page of this document. Sir, can you see that Gvero and this gentleman are addressed as "president", that Gvero addresses this gentleman as "president"? You agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. But he says president, vice-president, professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the participant in the conversation, who we can call Gvero, calls three persons he addresses "president"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes. I'm telling you yes, but there is a correction here. It says "president," "vice-president," "professor."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you have a look at this conversation, is Gvero informing Koljevic about his activities and about his discussions with UNPROFOR? Would you agree with me that that's what the conversation is about? I see you nodding but you should say it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: You asked me whether I can see from this document that he spoke to UNPROFOR members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This concerns relationships with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that's also the case for the intercepts that you recorded, the subject is the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Well, do you have the first one in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The first two that you recorded. Would you agree that the subject is the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-145
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, when it would be convenient, we passed the time to adjourn for today. Mr. Witness, unfortunately the Chamber has decided a long time ago that we need to break next week for a -- for the parties' preparation for the case. So we will resume Monday the 19th at 9.00. So I take it that you have to go back and come again. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
